en: Re-32601 – Śaivarahasya (Lalitāṣṭottara), Stotras.
Manuscript dimensions: 210 mm × 35 mm; 6–7 lines per folio.
The manuscript condition is poor;
ellipses (... are used to indicate missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters, while a question mark (? expresses doubt.
Letters in brackets are suggestions;
p = PDF page number;
f = number on the folio.

l = line number (p.1 title frame photo; p.2 bundle side-view photo; p.3a again title frame photo; p.3b folio broken, *śubham astu | avighnam astu*, ...*gaṇapataye namaḥ*; thereafter illegible) (p.4a blank; p.4b, f23a to 13a text in Telugu: *Lalitāṣṭottara*).

Salutations again and again to her who dwells upon the peak of the ruddy mountain; salutations... to her who is the fire to the great lineage of the Himālaya; salutations... to her whose beauty constitutes half the body of Śaṅkara; salutations again and again to her whose form is as pure as gleaming emerald; salutations again and again to her whose loveliness is the supreme excellence of the world; salutations again and again to her who is the beloved of the life-breath of the moon-crested Lord.

Salutations again and again to her whose single form is eternally fifteen years of age; salutations again and again to her who wears a crown and bracelets of rubies upon her face; salutations again and again to her whose forehead is adorned with a tilaka of musk; salutations again and again to her whose radiant head is marked with lines of sacred ash; salutations again and again to her whose eyes are like the petals of a full-blown lotus; salutations again and again to her whose nose has the luster of an autumnal Campaka flower.

Homage to her whose pair of golden earrings are swaying... Homage to her whose cheeks resemble jeweled mirrors... Homage to her whose smiling face is filled with betel... Homage to her whose teeth are like the seeds of a ripe pomegranate... Homage to her whose neck has a luster equal to a conch shell and a cluster of betel nuts... Homage to her.

Homage to her who possesses a magnificent, beautiful necklace of large pearls; homage to her who is the auspicious mistress of the noble son bound to the Lord of Mountains; homage to her whose lotus-hands shine with the lotus, noose, and goad; homage, homage to her whose glorious lotus-hands bestow the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; homage, homage to her [who holds] the flowers of the lotus, the kairava lily, and the mandāra.

Salutations again and again to her who shines like a pair of golden jars; salutations again and again to her whose four arms are beautiful and symmetrical; salutations again and again to her adorned with armlets; salutations again and again to her whose garments possess a beauty resembling lightning; salutations again and again to her whose hips are graced by a broad and shapely lower back.

Salutations again and again to her who is the essence of the erotic sentiment known through her auspicious beauty; salutations again and again to her who is delighted here by the gift of divine ornaments; salutations again and again to her whose lotus-feet possess qualities superior even to the *pārijāta* tree; salutations again and again to her whose feet are set within a cluster of excellent rubies; salutations again and again to her who dwells upon the great and auspicious throne of ten million *kāmakoṭis*; salutations again and again to her who is the moonlight for the night-lotus that is the eye of Śrīkaṇṭha.

Salutations again and again to her who is fanned by the celestial damsels with chowries; salutations again and again to her whose side-long glances possess the grace of protecting her devotees; salutations again and again to her whose limbs are covered in horripilation arising from the embrace of the Lord of the Earth; salutations again and again to her who gazes with side-long looks that give birth to the bodiless god of love; salutations again and again to her whose feet are colored by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Upendra; salutations again and again to her who is served by the foremost women of the immortals, headed by Śacī.

Salutations again and again to her who has fashioned the entire circle of the universe through her divine play; salutations again and again to her who is encompassed by the great powers beginning with Amṛtā; salutations again and again to her who bestows the sovereignty under a single umbrella; salutations again and again to her whose sandals are worshipped by Sanaka and the other sages; salutations again and again to her whose own majesty is praised by gods and seers; salutations again and again to her who is fully honored by Agastya and Dūrvāsas.

Salutations again and again to her who is affectionate toward the six-faced one whose face is like that of an elephant in rut; salutations again and again to her who dwells in the center of the great machine of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*); salutations again and again to her whose abundance is born from the sacrificial fire-pit of consciousness (*cidagni*); salutations again and again to her whose crown is joined with a crescent moon; salutations again and again to her whose gait is as graceful as that of a female swan in rut; salutations again and again to her who is worshipped by the multitude of people who bow before her.

Salutations again and again to her who bestows the fruit of bliss upon those whose faces are turned inward; salutations again and again to her who grants the desired fruits to women devoted to their husbands; salutations again and again to her who is filled with and overflowing with sincere compassion; salutations again and again to her who dwells in the midst of the great forest of lotuses; salutations again and again to her who is devoid of decrease, increase, or any excess of qualities; salutations again and again to her who is the witness of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

Salutations again and again to her who shatters the flood of great sins and minor transgressions... salutations again and again. Salutations again and again to her who destroys the delusion regarding the self within the physical body; salutations again and again to her who breaks the great terrors of malevolent spirits. Salutations again and again to her who dwells in the midst of the glorious sixteen-syllable mantra; salutations again and again to her whose divine form is born of herself, without beginning or end. Salutations... salutations to her who is separated from the primary [states] such as power (*śakti*), the *haṃsa*-pada, and so forth.

Salutations again and again to Lalitā, who is united with the circle of Mothers. Salutations again and again to her whose essential thread is fully established by all the Vedāntas. Salutations again and again to her who is skillful in severing the heads of cruel demons. Salutations again and again to her who bestows happiness upon the Lord of the Gods, who had fallen from his studenthood. Salutations again and again to her who destroys Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Niśumbha, and the others. Salutations again and again to her who instructs those such as Raktākṣa and Raktajihva.

Salutations again and again to her who subdued the power of the arms of the demon Mahiṣāsura. Salutations again and again to her who is the slayer of all wicked Danujas. Salutations again and again to her who is the cause of great enthusiasm for [the one with] cloud-like hair (*abhrakeśa*). Salutations again and again to her who is intent on dancing together with Maheśa. Salutations again and again to her who meditates upon the lotus-face of her own devotee. Salutations again and again to her who is the means for the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

Salutations again and again to her whose form is like that of the sister of Śrīnātha, whose limbs are firmly established... (l. 5) Salutations again and again to the one who destroys the distress of those devoted to Candraśekhara. (l. 6) Salutations again and again to the one whose consciousness is liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (p. 11a, l. 1) Salutations again and again to the one who grants the desired fruits through the recitation of her names. (l. 2) Salutations again and again to the one whose will effects creation, maintenance, and concealment. (l. 3) Salutations again and again to the one who attains perfection through the realization of the bull-bannered Lord (*Vṛṣabhadhvaja*).

Salutations to her who has shattered birth, death, old age, and disease; salutations again and again to her who is the treasure-house of detachment, devotion, and wisdom. Salutations again and again to her who destroys the sixfold group [of enemies], beginning with desire and anger; salutations again and again to her whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the king of kings. Salutations again and again to her who is the manifest, beautiful Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti; salutations again and again to her whose majesty is most highly honored in the foremost of horse-sacrifices.

Salutation to her who is adorned with a great arrow, sugarcane, and bow... salutation [to her]. Salutation, salutation to her who impels all gods and demons. Salutation, salutation to her whose abode is the lotus of the entire heart. Salutation, salutation to her whose residence is the unstruck great lotus. Salutation... salutation to her whose dwelling is the thousand-petaled lotus. Salutation, salutation to her who resides in the city free from rebirth.

Salutations to her who is praised by Vāṇī, Gāyatrī, and Sāvitrī; salutations... (salutations). Salutations to her whose lotus-feet are worshipped by Ramā and Bhūmi; salutations... (salutations). Salutations again and again to her whose glorious feet are honored by Lopāmudrā; ... (salutations). Salutations again and again to her whose body possesses the beauty of a thousand Ratis; salutations again and again. Salutations again and again to her whose heart is satisfied by mere contemplation.

Salutations again and again to her who bestows the accomplishment of a hundredfold perfect consciousness; salutations again and again to her who grants the fruit of the joy produced by Śrīlocana; salutations again and again to her who dwells in the center of the Jewel Island situated within the ocean of existence; salutations again and again to her who is eternally youthful and the auspiciousness of all auspicious things; salutations again and again to the illustrious Mahādevī, united with Mahādeva.

This hymn of one hundred and eight names of Giriśa and Girijā, spoken in its entirety by Vyāsa, which wards off all diseases, is recited daily by one who speaks with the voice of the mountain-dweller Śrīkaṇṭha; such a person obtains their desired fruit, the increase of longevity, sons... [and] without doubt attains the highest state.

Thus ends the *Śrī Śivarahasyaumāmaheśvarāṣṭottara*... [omitted]. May there be auspiciousness. Oṃ hrāṃ ... (oṃ hrīṃ) oṃ hrūṃ sphura ku... spṛ... tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa ... ha vama vama ghātaya ghātaya ... (jaya jaya) oṃ huṃ. Araṅgāya? huṃ. ... āṃ ... sta... paleyamasarvabha... [End of fragment]

(l.6) *ri* rakṣā rakṣā pratyaṅgire ............. (l.7) *rbhave bhuve pāhyatra ....................... (p.14a, l.1) *juṣāma lakṣmī namo va kirikebhyo .................. (l.2) *dra mahādevasuvratonnama svāhā । ........... (l.3) *tāstrāya svahakrī vikravikva...jahāsvaha ... (l.4) *vyomavyomāstra(strā)ya svāhā । ...........
(Blank) (p.14b, f1, may there be auspiciousness, may there be no obstacles, with the assistance of Mīnākṣī, l.1) Salutation to the illustrious Kaivalyaguru.
I bow to ... (bā)la; salutation to him. I bow to ... (hi) *Mādrināyakī. * (l.2) I bow to Su...nanayanā; I bow to Sundaranāyakī. (l.3)
The mother was as dark-green as an emerald, a Mātaṅgī woman full of passion.
May the auspicious lady who dwells in the Kadamba forest cast a sidelong glance upon us—
she whose excellent lotus-hands bear jeweled ornaments, O most noble one!
O you whose body is adorned with garlands, whose eyes are beautiful, and whose vessel is filled with sweetness!
In her whose face has conquered the moon, whose speech is worthy of praise, and who is herself to be saluted.
O Fish-eyed One, grant me devotion toward Nibha.

O Mother, [grant] to me that which arises from the meaning of the *upanaya*, which bestows fortune (*lakṣmī*), is skillful, whose waist is unshakeable, and who eternally [provides] for the three worlds—O embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss! 2.
Near a emerald gem, [she who is] the enemy of the God of Love;
(l.3) she who is skilled in the lore of training parrots held in her hand.
O Candrāvatamsā, mother of mine, shall I not go to that which is won by going? 3.
In the moon-like abode of Malaya, with the beauty of Mañjuka-stū...
[endowed] with various jewel ornaments, [he offered] the finest silk garment to his disciple.
O Mother, whose body possesses constant luster, whose petals are adorned with the Sāman [hymns], may you grant me prosperity.
O Mother, who dwells far within the heart, who fulfills all desired objects...
[in] the joy of Madana... [of] the body...
O Mother of mine!
O Goddess, beautiful in mind, may [he] perform the touching of water, fire, sky, moon, and light produced by jewels... in your presence.
O Mother, you are not at all full for me, even though you are filled with the hearts of those who have performed good deeds. 6.
Victory, victory to you, O Kadambā, who dwells upon the courtyard of the breast of Kṣīragaṃbā!
Victory, victory, victory to you, O Śīlā, who are worshipped by Viṣṇu from birth!
Victory, victory, victory to Śakti, the refuge for those who have taken birth! O Mother, [grant] me [your grace]. 7.
Victory to you, O Sumukha Kadamba, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
possessing the luster of a golden peak, and worthy of worship by Indra himself for the sake of bestowing wealth and the body.
O Mother, whose pair of lotus feet are as beautiful as the rising sun, [be] my refuge. 8.

Thus, whoever recites this *Aṣṭaka* with devotion shall obtain wealth and grain. He too shall always [attain] firm devotion to the feet of [the Lord], as well as longevity, health, [victory, and] the reality of Śaṅkara, the Lord of Pārvatī. O Leader of the city of Mathurā, salutations to you; O delight of Mathurā... in your hand. O daughter of the King of Pāṇḍya on Mount Malaya... O blessed Mīnākṣī, bestow your grace upon me. [Salutations to] the illustrious one accompanied by Mīnākṣī.

(p.16b, f3?, vighneśvarastotram, l.1) Of this great mantra, the Śrī Vighneśvarastotra... (l.2) Vighneśvara is the deity. For the purpose of [attaining] Vighneśvara, there is the application (*viniyoga*) in recitation (*japa*). (l.3) Nandikeśvara said: I bow my head to the god Vināyaka, the son of Gaurī.
One should constantly remember him with devotion for the sake of attaining long life... (l.4)
...the second is Daṃṣṭra;
the third is Vighnarājendra; the fourth is Karṇikā; the fifth is Lambodara;
the sixth is Vikaṭa; and the seventh is Viprarājendra.
Likewise, the eighth is Dhūmra-varṇa, and the ninth is Bālacandra;
the tenth is Vināyaka, the eleventh is Gaṇapati,
and the twelfth is Gajānana— thus are the twelve names.

The man who recites this at the three junctions of the day for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims obtains them; there is no doubt in this matter. Even one who is poor [obtains wealth], and he shall not see hell.
He is granted fearlessness from thieves and from the fangs of wild beasts.

For men, however, it brings about the destruction of [their] obstacles; one who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge, one who seeks wealth obtains wealth, and one who seeks a daughter obtains a daughter. One who seeks liberation obtains devotion.
One shall obtain the fruit [of this practice] within six months by means of this hymn to Gaṇapati.
One who seeks perfection (*siddhi*) obtains it within a year; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Vighnarāja-stotra in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara. (Indrākṣī, p. 17b, f4a, l. 1)

Of this great mantra, the Śrī Indrākṣī-stotra, [the Ṛṣi is] .................................... the metre is [Anuṣṭubh]. (l. 2) The deity is Indrākṣī. Lakṣmī is the seed-syllable. [The syllable] ........... is the *kīlaka*. (l. 3) The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the grace of Indrākṣī through recitation (*japa*). (l. 4) Salutation to Indrākṣī with the two thumbs. Salutation to Mahālakṣmī with the two index fingers. Salutation to Maheśvarī with the two middle fingers. (l. 5) Salutation to Ambujākṣī with the two ring fingers.

Salutation to Kātyāyanī with the two little fingers. (l. 6) Salutation to Kaumārī with the palms and backs of the hands. Salutation to Indra... for the heart. .......... (l. 7) Svāhā to the head. Vauṣaṭ to Maheśvarī for the crest-lock. Salutation to Ambujākṣī for the armor. (l. 8) Vauṣaṭ to Kātyāyanī for the three eyes. .................................. (p. 18a, l. 1) ...varom—thus is the binding of the directions. The visualization (dhyāna):
[She who is] surrounded by those whose eyes behold... [the fierce] Īśvarī. (l. 2)
I constantly meditate in my heart upon Hemāmbā— the great sovereign, white-crested and adorned with hair like pearls;
she whose pair of lotus-feet are honored by [the gods], whose breasts are like the frontal globes of the lord of elephants,
the Indrākṣī who bestows the perfection of truth.
The goddess Indrākṣī has two arms and is adorned with two garments;
she holds a vajra in her left hand and bestows boons with her right.
...a young woman adorned with various ornaments,
with a serene countenance, a Bhoja lady attended by hosts of Apsarases—
this is the queen named Indrākṣī...
...Rishashka... Rishi Devi Durga... ॥
To the enraged one...
[I offer] salutation to her; she is Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Brahmāṇī, and the expounder of Brahman.
Nārāyaṇī, Bhadrakālī, Rudrāṇī, Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā, Agnipālā, Raudramukhī, Sālarātrī, Tapasvinī,
Meghasvanā, Sahaprakṣī, Kaṭāṅgī, and Gaḍodarī.
Mahodarī, Muktakeśī, Ghorarūpā, Mahābalā, Ajitā, Bhadradānā, Tāroga-trī, Śivapriyā,
Śivadyuti, Karālī, and Pratyakṣaparameśvarī.
Indrāṇī, who possesses the form of Indra, is the supreme power of Indra;
she is the goddess who deludes the world, the mistress of the forest,
Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhī— [the goddesses] of terrible [forms].
Saci... Madhā, Vidyā-lakṣmī, Sarasvatī;
Anantā, Vijayā...nnā, Mānastoka...;
Bhavānī, Pārvatī, Durgā, Haimavatī, Ambikā, Śivā.
Śivā, Bhavānī, Rudrāṇī, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara—
those who [worship] each one of these goddesses are considered by me to have their desires fulfilled.
[She] causes fever to burn away the terrible fever of death, the destroyer of fevers.
...bestows suitable sovereignty and removes the fear of untimely death.
[It cures] consumption, leprosy, skin diseases, fever, and battle...
[one] is liberated from... || 6-7 ||
Turning [the mind] away from the bondage of disease...
[one attains] that fruit.
... there [was] Jarāstrī ...; ...
the wielder of the Śārṅga bow ... ॥
Then, having seen [him]... release your fever.
The devotee of Maheśvara and the devotee of Viṣṇu... engaged in combat. That devotee of Maheśvara, Mārkaṇḍeya, was [overpowered] by the strength of the devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having found no refuge elsewhere, the fever belonging to Maheśvara departed.
[When] the compassionate one... in Hari, Triśiras and Raktalocana, being equally pleased, may that fever, the lord of all diseases, grant happiness.
Homage to the Blessed One, Indrākṣī, who captivates the minds of all people;
she who, in the netherworld (*atala*) and here [on earth], [is] the crusher of the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura, whose form is like that of a bull.

[The one] who bestows great gifts, who removes the intoxication of pride and [other] seizures... [the one] who destroys the seizure of Skanda... [the one] who [destroys] the seizure of Kumāra, the seizure of children, the seizure of spirits (bhūta), the seizure of Śālā... the seizure of Gaṇḍa... [and so forth]. May [it] ward off for me the pain in the head, the pain in the ears, the pain in the sides, the pain in the belly, the jaundice... [and] the nine [fevers]... svāhā. [The remainder of the page is blank. [On folio 7a, the Śivakavaca begins: Homage to the Vajra-evil one. Homage to Nīlakaṇṭha... [and so forth].

Having paid homage with speech... I shall speak of the auspicious [teaching] that brings about protection... having prepared a seat, with senses conquered... he who meditates on the imperishable Śiva, seated within the lotus of the heart, who has pervaded the space by his own splendor... I meditate upon Maheśa, who is without support, subtle, infinite, primordial, and composed of consciousness.

O you whose bonds of all phenomena have been shaken off by meditation, may you—whose self is composed through the *nyāsa* [of mantras] for the sake of the long-lasting bliss of consciousness—perform protection with the armor (*kavaca*) of Śiva. May you, whose essence is the deity, protect me... You are said to be the root for one fallen into the deep well of *saṃsāra*. May you shake off what resides in my heart... May your form protect me everywhere.

May the one Lord of all, who is composed of light, a mass of bliss, the conscious self, subtler than the subtlest, possessing manifold powers, protect [us] from every fear. May he who, in the form of the universe, protects through devotion, and who on earth as the Lord of the Mountain (*Girīśa*) possesses eight forms, protect the world. May he who acts toward men in his various aspects protect that living being from the *kalas* (portions of time). May the Lord of the Hand (*Pāṇīśa*), whose eyes are fixed upon him, dance... [for his protection].

He, Kālarudra... [is] worshipped first by [those beginning with] ...fear. With a lamp... blazing forth... holding an axe in his hand; four-faced, that Tatpuruṣa, three-eyed... standing on the right, may he protect me from fatigue. (L. 4) Holding an axe, a Veda... a *kuśa*-grass noose, a trident, a skull, and emitting sparks of fire... (L. 5) Four-faced, blue... three-eyed; may that foremost of gods protect me in the southern direction. (L. 6) White as a jasmine flower, the moon, a conch shell, or crystal...

[He who holds] a rosary, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*)... who is three-eyed and four-faced, by whose great power [the goddesses] Sadyojātā and the others are considered [manifested]... [he] whose lotus-hands hold a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and an axe, [and who is] of uniform color. May the three-eyed, four-faced Vāmadeva protect me in the northern direction—he whose hands hold the Vedas, the gesture of fearlessness, the *iṣṭā* (sacrificial vessel), a *kuśa*-grass ring, a water-pot, a drum (*ḍhakka*), an eye, a trident, and a discus, and who possesses five faces of white radiance.

May he whose head is Īśāna, whose head is supreme light, protect my forehead; may he whose eyes are wide-open protect my eyes; may he whose purpose is his own self always protect my nose; may he whose form is beautiful protect my ears; may Śakra, together with his wife, protect my eyebrows; and may Dharmabāhu protect us from the very root of our feet.

May the Destroyer of Madana protect my chest; may the Lord of the Mountain-king protect my right arm; may He who is the end-maker of Madana protect my middle part. May Heramba protect your side for the sake of my protection; may the Smoky One protect my waist; may the Lord be mine. May Varuṇa protect my two thighs; may the Friend of Mitra protect [my knees]; may the Lord of the World protect my two knees; may the Bull-bannered One protect my pair of shanks. May He whose feet are worshipped by the gods protect my feet; may Maheśvara protect me during the first watch of the day.

May [the Lord] protect me in the middle...; may the Bull-bannered One protect me in the third watch; may the Moon-crested One protect me during the night; may Gaṅgādhara protect me at the end of the night; may Mṛtyuñjaya protect me for all time; protecting me as I abide within, may Śaṅkara always protect me as I abide outside.

Immediately thereafter, may the Lord of Beasts, Sadāśiva, protect me on all sides. May the One Lord of many masters protect me while I stand...; may the Lord of the Pramathas protect me as I walk. May [He] protect me while seated, desiring Śiva through the Vedānta...; may [He] protect me while traveling. On the paths, may the Blue-throated One protect me; in the mountain fastnesses, may Akṣa... protect me.

Dwelling in the forest... possessing the noble power of the fragrance of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)... at the time of the fierce wrath of the black cloth... alas! his testicles are ablaze. He who is like Indra, a hero whose sacrifice is protected by crocodiles and serpents, and who is as difficult to restrain as the ocean of the enemy army of the Earth. May he—[who] leaps upon the herds of elephants that have turned back, [and] is adorned with millions of weapons for protection—a hundred times a hundred Akṣauhiṇīs of attacking lords—cut [them down] with the terrible stream of his... sword.

It slays the *dasyus* as if with a trident, the weapon of the Destroyer of Tripura. O bow of the Lord, cause the tigers, lions, bears, deer, and [other] beasts to tremble! [Drive away] the ill omens in dreams, famine, misfortunes, and the portents that afflict the ruler. Repeatedly dispel the fear of poison, and may disease be destroyed for me by [the power of] Śiva.

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, to Sadāśiva, who consists of all principles (*tattva*), who is known by all principles, who is the sole mouth of all the worlds, whose body is [all]... the destroyer of all... the sole teacher of all enjoyments, the destroyer of all... the secret of all the Vedas (*nigama*), the sole... of all the worlds, [the destroyer] of all misfortunes and so forth.

To the one whose crest is [the moon], the eternal, for the sake of one’s own manifestation, for the sake of [liberation]... for the sake of the one who is free from fear, who is without a bow, who is beyond conceptual proliferation, who is without limbs... to the one devoid of qualities, devoid of [defilements], eternally pure, awakened, and perfectly complete... to the supreme light of the non-dual ocean of consciousness, whose form is splendor... to Rudra, Mahārudra, Kālabhairava...

Wearing a garland of skulls and a *khaṭvāṅga*, [holding] a noose... a bow... a *bhiṇḍipāla*... with a terrifying face made formidable by fangs like the weapons of Śakra and the other gods... adorned with the coils of the lords of serpents and the ornaments of serpent-kings... wearing the skin of the lord of serpents... [who is] like Tryambaka, Sadāśiva, Viśveśvara, Virūpākṣa, and the bull-vehicled [Śiva].

O you who blaze with faces on all sides and mouths facing every direction, destroy the fear of untimely death; drive away the fear of poison and serpents; O Ramā... slay my enemies... [obscured]... by the root-mantra, pierce, pierce them with the sword...

Drink! Understand! Crush with the root-mantra! ... terrify! Satrāsaya! ... O you, terrify, terrify! Cause to give, cause to give! O Kūṣmāṇḍa... and the hosts of Brahma-rākṣasas, terrify, terrify me! Grant me, grant me fearlessness! Comfort me, who am terrified, comfort me! ... gladden, gladden... afflicted by heat...

Protect me from the fear of hell; lift me up, lift me up! Cover me, cover me with the auspicious armor (*śivakavaca*). O Mṛtyuñjaya, Tryambaka, Sadāśiva, salutations to you, salutations... [O] Ṛṣabha. This supreme armor (*kavaca*), which I have proclaimed, has been declared as the secret that pacifies all afflictions for all embodied beings.
